fields.description: Eight months into the job and a year into living in Port Alder, you are good with engines, careful with money and still learning the town's unwritten rules. You rent 2B above the hardware store, make payments on a pickup older than it looks, and keep an old fishing boat on a trailer at the marina for days off.
Heavy-set, patient and fond of old pickup trucks. He built the shop up over eleven years, remembers every customer's name and keeps a lot of his worries to himself.
Funny, quick with a wrench and a little too keen on being the one who knows how to fix things. He has worked at the shop six years and lives in 2A, across the landing from you.
Organized, warm and permanently carrying a clipboard. She keeps the township's books, runs the festival committee and is quietly hoping someone will volunteer to help.

fields.description: Dry-witted, sharp with names and pouring a pint faster than anyone in town. She lives in 1A with her grandmother and her fifteen-year-old sister, Maddie, and is saving to start a boat-charter business of her own.

Fifteen, quick and a little too observant, Jess's kid sister is a sophomore at Lakeshore Consolidated. She lives in 1A with Jess and their grandmother, rides to school on the morning bus, and spends her free hours at the coffee shop or hanging around the marina dock.
Weathered, deliberate and usually wearing a faded cap from a long-closed tackle shop. He has run the marina for twenty-five years and is happiest when someone asks him how to read the lake.
Small, firm and fond of crossword puzzles and the ball game on the radio. She has owned the building for forty years, keeps the rents low and knows every tenant's footsteps on the stairs.

fields.description: Tired, funny and endlessly practical. She works three twelve-hour shifts a week, lives alone with a very old cat, and would like very much to sleep through one entire Saturday.

fields.description: Calm, dry and good at finding the lost dog in under an hour. Sam works the afternoon shift and knows who is parked where in this town.

A midsize pickup with a faded paint job and a rattle you know the source of but haven't fixed. Financed through the credit union.
A used utility ATV bought for cash last spring. It lives in the back bay at the shop.

A scuffed 18-foot outboard fishing boat that came to you in trade for an engine overhaul on a customer's account. It sits on a trailer in the yard by Dale's boat ramp, and you launch it when you want the lake.
A 22-foot pontoon with a tired outboard, a bimini top and a faded cushion on every seat. It runs when it feels like it.
A heavy-duty diesel with a flatbed and a winch. Marcus names it something different every year.
A white full-size pickup with the township seal on the door. It cranks and cranks and does not catch.
A long strip of dunes, orchards and small harbor towns on the east shore of Lake Michigan.
A harbor town of about 6,500 people with a brick Main Street, a working marina, two stoplights and an unreasonable number of coffee shops in summer.
A three-storey brick building with Harbor Hardware on the ground floor and four apartments above. Unit 2B has a lake view if you lean out of the bathroom window.
A three-bay repair shop on Lake Avenue with a customer counter, a parts shelf and a back lot full of cars waiting for one more part. The radio is always on.
A waterfront bar and grill with a deck over the harbor, a wall of old buoys and the best burger in the county. Trivia is on Thursdays.
A bright corner cafe on Main Street with mismatched chairs, a good espresso machine and a pastry case that empties by ten.
A low brick building with a flagpole and a bulletin board. Permits, tax bills and the township's vehicle yard are all handled here.
A one-storey clinic with urgent care, a pharmacy window and a waiting room that smells of hand sanitizer and old magazines.
Eighty slips, a boat ramp, a fuel dock and a barn full of winter storage. The harbor office has a bell on the door and a coffee pot that is never quite empty.
A strip of beach, lawn and picnic tables beside the marina. The pavilion hosts the weekly farmers' market in summer and Harbor Fest in September.
The town's only full grocery store, with a deli counter, a rack of local apples and a bulletin board covered in lost-cat flyers.
A gas station and convenience store on the road out of town, with four pumps, a car wash and surprisingly good hot dogs.

Twelve miles of marked sand trails through the dunes, open to ATVs and side-by-sides from a trailhead lot off County Road 12. The sand is deep, the views are huge and the rules are posted on a sign no one reads.
A wooded island six kilometers offshore with a lighthouse, a small campground and a ferry that runs from the marina several times a day in season.
The nearest big city, about a three-and-a-half-hour drive around the bottom of the lake, in the Central time zone: an hour behind Port Alder.

A low brick school on the edge of town that serves Port Alder and the farms behind the dunes: one long corridor, a gym that doubles as the auditorium, and a flagpole in front. Classes run from eight until ten past three.

basis.summary: Rounded, approximate state-level figures compiled from well-known public statistics as recalled; not queried live. Intended as plausible defaults, not as authoritative statistics.
basis.state_income_tax_effective_pct: Approximate effective state income tax as a percent of gross wages for a single filer earning about $60,000 (a middle-income band), after the state standard deduction/exemptions; derived from published 2025 state brackets (Tax Foundation / state revenue departments). Rounded to 0.1. Excludes local income taxes (see local_income_tax_pct_typical) and payroll-type state levies such as CA SDI.
basis.sales_tax_combined_avg_pct: Tax Foundation 2025 combined state plus population-weighted average local sales tax rate; rounded to 0.01. Hawaii and Alaska values are approximations of the GET / local-only rate.
basis.cost_of_living_multiplier: US = 1.00. Approximate from BEA Regional Price Parities (all items, 2022-2023 vintage) smoothed to 2025; rounded to 0.01.
basis.median_rent_cents_per_month: Approximate asking-rent medians for 1BR and 2BR units, a blend of Zumper, Apartment List and HUD FY2025 Fair Market Rent state patterns, rounded to $10. 1BR is the anchor; 2BR is derived as 1BR times a regional ratio (Northeast 1.22, Midwest 1.27, South 1.27, West 1.24; DC uses South) rounded to $10. Statewide medians hide large metro-vs-rural spread.
basis.residential_electricity_cents_per_kwh: EIA Electric Power Monthly, average residential retail price by state, 2024 annual / 2025 year-to-date, rounded to 0.5 cent. Decimal value in cents (not dollars) per kWh. US average is about 17 cents.
basis.minimum_wage_cents_per_hour: Effective statutory floor in 2025 for non-tipped adult workers: the higher of the state rate and the federal $7.25. Where rates vary by locality or employer size (NY, OR, MN) the statewide/largest-area figure is used.

scope.doc: `national` is the single baseline row `us` (multiplier 1.00); the state-only columns are absent on it.

state_income_tax_effective_pct.doc: Single filer at about $60,000, after the state standard deduction; excludes local and payroll levies.

cost_of_living_multiplier.doc: US = 1.00. Applied by the economy pack at pricing time, never baked into rows.

minimum_wage_cents_per_h.doc: Effective 2025 floor, the higher of state and federal.

minimum_payment.formula: min(statement_balance + interest + fees, max(floor_cents, ceil(statement_balance * principal_pct / 100 + interest_this_cycle + fees_this_cycle)))

2% of balance, no extra interest add-on

high_yield.note: Online banks; floating with the Fed funds rate.

investing.title: Investing (index return model, GBM recipe, bonds, cash)

broad_us_equity_index.description: Total-return broad US stock index (S&P 500 style) for seeded price paths; use geometric Brownian motion with these parameters.
broad_us_equity_index.long_run_basis: 1926-2024 nominal total return ~10% geometric, ~12% arithmetic, ~19% volatility; modern-era (post-1990) volatility ~15-17%; the typical 5-year-ahead expectation is lower, ~6-8% nominal.
broad_us_equity_index.gbm_note: S(t+dt) = S(t) * exp((mu - sigma^2/2) dt + sigma sqrt(dt) Z) with mu=0.11, sigma=0.16 per year; use a seeded RNG.

retirement_account_limits_cents.note: IRS limits for 2025; 2026 values as announced in IRS Notice 2025-67 (401(k) $24,500, catch-up $8,000, IRA $7,500).

single.note: KFF 2025: average worker contribution ~$1,440/yr (about 16% of a ~$9,300 premium) for single coverage.

family.note: KFF 2025: average worker contribution ~$6,850/yr (~26% of a ~$27,000 premium).

compact_car.name: Compact car (Civic / Corolla class)
compact_car.notes: US new-vehicle average transaction price is near $49,000 in 2025 across all classes; compacts are at the low end.

pickup_midsize.name: Midsize pickup (Tacoma / Colorado class)
pickup_midsize.notes: Cargo is the open bed (about 5 ft). Towing about 6,500 lb.

pickup_fullsize.name: Full-size pickup (F-150 / Silverado class)
pickup_fullsize.notes: Cargo is the open bed (5.5-6.5 ft). Towing up to ~10,000 lb with the right package.

pickup_heavy_duty_diesel.name: Heavy-duty diesel pickup (2500 / F-250 class)
pickup_heavy_duty_diesel.notes: DEF fluid (diesel exhaust fluid) refills every ~5,000 miles, about $15-25/ 2.5 gal. Towing up to 15,000-20,000 lb.

suv_compact.name: Compact SUV (RAV4 / CR-V class)
suv_compact.notes: Cargo volume is with the rear seats folded: about 1,100 L; behind seats about 540 L. Hybrids reach 38-41 mpg.

suv_midsize_3row.name: Midsize three-row SUV (Highlander / Explorer class)
suv_midsize_3row.notes: Cargo with second and third rows folded about 2,300 L; behind the third row about 480 L.

minivan.name: Minivan (Sienna / Odyssey / Pacifica class)
minivan.notes: Hybrid minivans (Sienna) return 35-36 mpg combined; cargo with rows folded is about 4,000 L (140 cu ft).

ev_sedan.name: Electric sedan (Model 3 / Ioniq 6 class)
ev_sedan.notes: No oil changes. Many states add an EV registration surcharge of about $100-$250 per year, included in the registration band. Tires wear faster (instant torque, weight).

ev_crossover.name: Electric crossover (Model Y / Equinox EV class)
ev_crossover.notes: Cargo volume with rear seats folded.

motorcycle_standard.name: Motorcycle, standard or cruiser (500-900 cc)
motorcycle_standard.notes: Cargo is saddlebags or a tail bag; a passenger seat is optional. Front/rear tires are replaced separately (rear wears ~2x faster). Helmet laws vary by state.

scooter_150.name: Scooter or moped (50-150 cc)
scooter_150.notes: Under-seat storage about 25-35 L. Mopeds under 50 cc often need no registration or license in some states; top speed 30-60 mph.

bass_boat_outboard.name: Outboard bass boat (18-20 ft, 150-200 hp)

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil, filters and lower-unit gear oil every 100 hours or annually

bass_boat_outboard.notes: Boat state registration usually renews every 1-3 years (annualised here); trailer is registered separately (~$30-$100/year). Price includes motor and trailer. Cruise burn is at planing speed with a normal load.

pontoon_boat.name: Pontoon boat (22-24 ft, 90-150 hp outboard)
pontoon_boat.notes: Capacity plate typically 8-13 persons / 1,500-2,500 lb total.

jet_ski_pwc.name: Personal watercraft / jet ski (1-3 seats)

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil and filter every 50 hours or annually

jet_ski_pwc.notes: Premium-grade fuel recommended by most makers. Price excludes trailer ($800-$2,500).

sailboat_auxiliary.name: Cruising sailboat with auxiliary diesel (30-35 ft)

consumption.note: Displacement hull: motors at hull speed (~6 knots) burning 0.6-1.0 gph; sailing uses no fuel.

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil and filters every 100-150 hours; impeller every 200 hours

sailboat_auxiliary.notes: Documented vessels (US Coast Guard documentation) pay no state registration. A rule of thumb is that ownership costs 10% of value per year. Sleeps 4-6.

atv_utility.name: ATV, utility quad (450-700 cc)
atv_utility.notes: Cargo: front and rear racks, about 40 kg front and 80 kg rear. Many states require an off-highway vehicle (OHV) sticker/permit rather than road registration; helmet and age rules vary.

utv_side_by_side.name: UTV / side-by-side (Ranger / RZR class, 2-4 seats)
utv_side_by_side.notes: Utility models carry a dump bed up to ~450 kg; sport models carry people only. Roll cage and belts required.

dirt_bike_250.name: Dirt bike, 250 cc four-stroke
dirt_bike_250.notes: Competition bikes are not street legal; plated dual-sport bikes use the motorcycle class. Premium fuel with 91+ octane typical.

factors.doc: Factor id to consumption multiplier (>1 burns more). Road: relative to the combined rating; marine: to cruise_planing; off-road: to normal_trail.

road.basis: Multipliers on fuel (or energy) consumed per mile relative to the combined rating; >1 burns more. Rounded rules of thumb from EPA/fueleconomy.gov and AAA tests.
road.note: For EVs the same multipliers apply to kWh per mile (cold weather is harsher: use 1.35; highway 75 mph: 1.30; towing: 2.0).

marine.basis: Multipliers on gallons per hour at planing cruise; rules of thumb from engine makers' fuel curves (Mercury, Yamaha, Volvo Penta) and BoatUS guidance.
marine.note: Plan on the 1/3 out, 1/3 back, 1/3 reserve fuel rule. Marine tank capacities are usable gallons.

offroad.basis: Multipliers on gallons per hour at normal trail pace; rule-of-thumb values from OEM spec sheets and trail-riding reports.

lore_port_alder.title: Port Alder
lore_port_alder.content: Port Alder sits on the east shore of Lake Michigan with about 6,500 residents. It began as a lumber port, became a fruit-shipping town and is now mostly a place where people fish, sail, ride dune buggies and commute to somewhere larger. It has two stoplights, one high school and no tolerance for being called quaint.

lore_harbor_street.title: 114 Harbor Street
lore_harbor_street.content: 114 Harbor Street is a brick building with Harbor Hardware on the ground floor and four apartments above. Helen Kowalczyk has owned it for forty years and keeps the rents under what the neighbors charge. The stairs creak on the ninth step, and everyone on the second floor knows who is coming home.

lore_shop.title: Alder Automotive
lore_shop.content: Alder Automotive has three bays, a counter, a parts shelf and a back lot of cars waiting for a part. Marcus Delgado opened it eleven years ago. It repairs everything from boat trailers to the township's tractors and is the first place locals call when a tow is needed.

lore_anchor.title: The Rusty Anchor
lore_anchor.content: The Rusty Anchor is the local bar and grill. It has a deck over the harbor, a wall of old buoys, a pool table with a wobbly leg and a Thursday trivia night that gets competitive. The burger is excellent. The jukebox only plays a handful of songs, and everyone knows them all.

lore_bluebird.title: Bluebird Coffee
lore_bluebird.content: Bluebird Coffee is a bright corner cafe on Main Street with a good espresso machine, an overworked barista and a pastry case that empties by ten. A drip coffee costs three dollars; a latte costs about six. Half the town's business is conducted at its mismatched tables.

lore_township_hall.title: Alder Township Hall
lore_township_hall.content: The township handles permits, property taxes, the vehicle yard and the festival fund. Its staff is small and overworked: an accountant, a clerk, a supervisor and a handful of part-timers. It owns a fleet of aging trucks that are serviced wherever the lowest bidder is this year.

lore_clinic.title: Alder Community Clinic
lore_clinic.content: A one-storey clinic with urgent care, primary care and a pharmacy window. It covers most of what a small town needs, and sends the rest to a hospital forty minutes away. Staff are friendly, the waiting room is cold, and the vending machine is always out of the good snack.

lore_marina.title: Alder Harbor Marina
lore_marina.content: The marina has eighty slips, a boat ramp, a fuel dock and a barn for winter storage. Dale Whitcomb has run it for twenty-five years. In season, a slip rents by the month; for guests, a night at the dock is cheap and the coffee in the office is free. Dale lets a few regulars keep a trailered boat in the yard by the ramp, and launches it for them on request.

lore_park.title: Lakefront Park
lore_park.content: A strip of beach, lawn and picnic tables beside the marina, with a pavilion that hosts the farmers' market on summer Saturdays. It fills up on the Fourth of July and on the fourth weekend of September for Harbor Fest.

lore_market.title: Alder Market
lore_market.content: The only full grocery store in town carries what you need, a few things you don't and a rack of local apples in fall. Its bulletin board advertises everything from lost cats to dune-buggy repairs. Prices run a little under national averages.

lore_fuel.title: Shoreline Fuel
lore_fuel.content: Shoreline Fuel has four pumps, a car wash and a rotating selection of hot dogs. Regular gasoline runs about three dollars and fifteen cents a gallon. It is open from five in the morning until eleven at night and is the first place anyone stops after a flat tire.

lore_dunes.title: Shoreline Dunes Trail System
lore_dunes.content: Twelve miles of marked sand trails run through the dunes, open to ATVs and side-by-sides from a trailhead off County Road 12. Riders must stay on the marked trail, wear helmets, and keep an eye on the weather: a front can roll off the lake in minutes.

lore_gull_island.title: Gull Island State Park
lore_gull_island.content: Gull Island has a lighthouse, a small campground and a long shingle beach. A ferry from the marina makes the crossing in about twenty-five minutes, several times a day in season, and costs around nine dollars. It does not run when the wind is up.

lore_harbor_fest.title: Harbor Fest
lore_harbor_fest.content: Harbor Fest is held on the fourth Saturday of September. It has food stalls, a brass band, a pie contest and a parade of decorated boats at two in the afternoon. The township's festival fund pays for most of it, and Priya Nair has organized it for the last four years.

lore_marcus.title: Marcus Delgado
lore_marcus.content: Marcus Delgado owns Alder Automotive. He is fifty-two, heavy-set and patient, and fixes everything slowly and well. Employees say he never raises his voice and never forgets a mistake. He works longer hours than any of them.

lore_danny.title: Danny Okafor
lore_danny.content: Danny Okafor is the shop's senior mechanic. Thirty-one, funny and fast, he knows every engine in town by its sound. He lives in 2A and tells everyone he has no plans to leave Port Alder, though he drives down to Chicago to see his family when the shop can spare him. He is competitive in a way he thinks is invisible.

lore_priya.title: Priya Nair
lore_priya.content: Priya Nair is the township accountant and Harbor Fest's organizer. She is warm, brisk and permanently holding a clipboard. She can tell you the festival budget to the dollar and the name of every vendor's cousin.

lore_jess.title: Jess Kowalczyk
lore_jess.content: Jess Kowalczyk tends bar at the Rusty Anchor five nights a week. Twenty-four, dry-witted and exact with a pour, she lives in 1A with her grandmother and her kid sister Maddie, and spends her days off looking at boats she cannot yet afford.

lore_maddie.title: Maddie Kowalczyk
lore_maddie.content: Maddie Kowalczyk is fifteen, Jess's kid sister, and a sophomore at Lakeshore Consolidated. She walks to the bus on school mornings, does her homework at the Bluebird Coffee shop twice a week and spends Friday afternoons on the marina dock, where Dale lets her coil lines in return for a lesson now and then.

lore_school.title: Lakeshore Consolidated School
lore_school.content: Lakeshore Consolidated serves Port Alder and the farms behind the dunes. The fall term began on Monday 31 August and runs to Friday 20 November; the school closes for Thanksgiving week, reopens on Monday 30 November and lets out for winter break after Friday 18 December. Classes run from eight o'clock until ten past three.

lore_dale.title: Dale Whitcomb
lore_dale.content: Dale Whitcomb owns the marina. Sixty-one, weathered and unhurried, he is happiest when someone asks him how to read the lake. He lends boats to people he trusts, and has strong opinions about the people he does not.

lore_helen.title: Helen Kowalczyk
lore_helen.content: Helen Kowalczyk, seventy-one, owns 114 Harbor Street and has lived on its ground floor for forty years. She is firm, kind, nosy in equal measure, and still does the crossword in pen.

lore_nora.title: Nora Whitfield
lore_nora.content: Nora Whitfield is a nurse at the clinic. She works three twelve-hour shifts a week, lives alone with an elderly cat, and is the person to ask about any medical question at three in the morning.

lore_sam.title: Sam Reyes
lore_sam.content: Officer Sam Reyes works the afternoon patrol. Calm and dry, Sam is more likely to resolve a dispute with a conversation than a ticket, and has found the missing dog in less than an hour more times than anyone can count.

lore_lake.title: The lake
lore_lake.content: Lake Michigan is calm for weeks and then, with almost no warning, isn't. Locals check the marine forecast before they put a boat in the water, and the marina flies a pennant when a small-craft advisory is in force.

lore_cost_of_living.title: Living in Port Alder
lore_cost_of_living.content: Port Alder is cheaper than most of the country: a one-bedroom rents for about eleven hundred dollars a month, groceries cost a little under the national average and electricity runs close to twenty cents a kilowatt-hour. A mechanic makes about twenty-four dollars an hour and a nurse about forty-five.

currency.note: Money is integer cents. National prices are scaled by the region's cost-of-living multiplier (Michigan 0.95) at pricing time.
